units.title: Unit 91 — Expressions with get
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 91. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise basic and specialised meanings of get in informal spoken English.
Distinguish key get phrasal verbs by meaning, context and grammatical pattern.
Use idiomatic get expressions naturally and interpret related exercise contrasts.

items.example: I got a message from the supplier this morning.
items.note: Get often means receive in everyday spoken English.

items.example: Could you get some bread on your way home?
items.note: In a shopping context, get can mean buy or obtain.

items.pt: chegar em casa; voltar para casa
items.example: How will the visitors get home after the concert?
items.note: Get can describe movement or reaching a destination; get home takes no to.

items.example: The patient's condition is slowly getting better.
items.note: Get plus an adjective can express a change of state.

items.example: I'll get dinner ready while you finish your assignment.
items.note: Get dinner can mean prepare a meal, not necessarily buy it.

items.example: I read the explanation twice, but I still don't get it.
items.note: An informal way of saying understand something.

items.example: The constant interruptions really get me.
items.note: Get someone can informally mean annoy or upset them.

items.pt: conseguir fazer; ter a oportunidade de fazer
items.example: I finally got to meet the new research director.
items.note: Get to do something can mean have the chance or manage to do it.

items.example: It takes time to get to know a new colleague.
items.note: Describes the gradual process of becoming acquainted with someone.

items.example: Could you get the phone while I wash my hands?
items.note: An informal instruction to answer a ringing phone.

items.example: Someone is knocking; I'll get the door.
items.note: Means answer the door when someone arrives.

items.example: She used a diagram to get her argument across.
items.note: Get an idea across means communicate it successfully to other people.

items.example: The investigation is trying to get at the cause of the fault.
items.note: Here, get at means reach or uncover information that is difficult to find.

items.example: I got behind with my coursework after missing two classes.
items.note: Describes failing to keep up with work or commitments.

items.example: Weeks of grey weather can really get people down.
items.note: Get someone down means make someone unhappy or discouraged.

items.pt: começar a se dedicar seriamente a
items.example: We need to get down to preparing the technical report.
items.note: Get down to is followed by a noun or -ing form, not a bare infinitive.

items.example: She worked hard to get into a competitive university.
items.note: Get into a university or school means be accepted as a student.

items.example: How are you getting on without a car?
items.note: Here, get on means manage or cope in a situation.

items.example: My younger brother is getting on well with his studies.
items.note: Here, get on means make progress or develop.

items.example: He tried to get out of attending the compulsory meeting.
items.note: Get out of an obligation can mean avoid doing something expected of you.

items.example: It took her several weeks to get over the illness.
items.note: Get over a difficulty or illness means recover from it.

items.example: Word of the promotion quickly got round the office.
items.note: In this sense, get round describes news spreading among people.

items.example: I still haven't got round to updating my CV.
items.note: Get round to is normally followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.pt: ser aprovado em; concluir com sucesso
items.example: Everyone in the group got through the final assessment.
items.note: Here, get through means successfully complete a difficult task or examination.

items.example: We got through most of our supplies during the first week.
items.note: Here, get through means use up an amount of something.

items.example: The children are unusually quiet; what are they getting up to?
items.note: Often suggests that someone, especially a child, is doing something mischievous.

items.word: get out of bed on the wrong side
items.example: He's been complaining all morning; he must have got out of bed on the wrong side.
items.note: An informal idiom describing someone who starts the day in a bad mood.

items.word: get off to a good start
items.example: The new project got off to a good start with a clear plan.
items.note: Get off to a good or bad start describes how something begins.

items.word: get off to a bad start
items.example: The interview got off to a bad start when the video call failed.
items.note: A natural contrast to get off to a good start.

items.example: We're organising a small get-together for the new team members.
items.note: A noun for an informal social meeting or party.

items.example: We should get rid of the obsolete equipment.
items.note: Means remove or dispose of something unwanted.

items.example: She was determined to get her own back after the unfair joke.
items.note: An informal expression for taking revenge on someone.

items.pt: avançar para; passar para uma etapa
items.example: He got through to the last round of interviews.
items.note: With to, get through can refer to advancing to the next stage of a selection process.

items.example: What have you been getting up to during your holiday?
items.note: In friendly conversation, this can simply ask what someone has been doing, without implying wrongdoing.

units.title: Unit 92 — Expressions with set and put
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 92. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish meanings of set and put phrasal verbs through their objects and context.
Use particle choices and complements accurately in frequent spoken and written expressions.
Understand idiomatic set/put expressions and their more formal equivalents.

items.example: We set aside part of our income for unexpected expenses.
items.note: Set aside money means save or reserve it for a particular purpose.

items.example: They set off before sunrise to avoid the traffic.
items.note: In this sense, set off is intransitive and means begin a journey.

items.pt: começar com um objetivo; propor-se a
items.example: The researchers set out to test a new hypothesis.
items.note: Set out to do something expresses a specific purpose or intention.

items.example: The alarm was set off by a sudden vibration.
items.note: Transitive set off means cause an event or reaction to start.

items.example: They plan to set up a small engineering consultancy.
items.note: Set up a business or organisation means establish it.

items.example: Try to set aside your personal preferences when reviewing the proposal.
items.note: Here, set aside means temporarily ignore a feeling or concern.

items.example: The committee put forward several practical suggestions.
items.note: Put forward an idea or proposal means present it for consideration.

items.example: She put herself forward for election to the student council.
items.note: Put yourself forward means offer yourself as a candidate.

items.example: All applicants must put in their forms by Friday.
items.note: Here, put in means submit a form, request or application.

items.example: The presenter put her main ideas across very clearly.
items.note: Put ideas across means communicate them effectively.

items.example: He constantly puts his colleagues down in meetings.
items.note: Put someone down means make them feel or appear inferior.

items.example: She put in a quick remark before the discussion ended.
items.note: Put in a remark means add a comment to a conversation.

items.example: The landlord agreed to put in a new heating system.
items.note: Here, put in means install equipment or fittings.

items.example: I put the desk together using the instructions.
items.note: Put together means assemble something from parts.

items.example: The drama group is putting on a play next month.
items.note: Put on a performance or event means organise and present it.

items.example: I hope my late arrival won't put you out.
items.note: Put someone out means inconvenience them.

items.example: Please put the tools away when you've finished.
items.note: Put something away means return it to its proper place.

items.example: My cousins offered to put me up for the weekend.
items.note: Put someone up means provide temporary accommodation.

items.example: We had to put off the inspection until Monday.
items.note: Put off an appointment, decision or event means postpone it.

items.example: The club plans to put up its membership fees.
items.note: Here, put up means raise prices, fees or other amounts.

items.example: They put up notices in every corridor.
items.note: Put up a notice or poster means display it on a surface.

items.example: She put on a Scottish accent for the comedy sketch.
items.note: Here, put on means pretend to have a voice, accent or manner.

items.example: Loud conversations put me off when I'm reading.
items.note: Put someone off can mean distract them from what they are doing.

items.example: I won't put up with repeated interruptions during meetings.
items.note: Put up with someone or something means tolerate unpleasant behaviour or conditions.

items.example: She's set her heart on studying abroad next year.
items.note: Set your heart on something means want it strongly; on takes a noun or -ing form.

items.example: He's set his sights on becoming a team leader.
items.note: Set your sights on something expresses an ambitious personal objective.

items.example: I've set myself a target of reading two books a month.
items.note: The standard pattern is set yourself a target of plus a noun or -ing form.

items.pt: discutir como resolver os problemas do mundo
items.example: They stayed up late setting the world to rights over coffee.
items.note: Usually describes informal discussion about problems and how things should change.

items.pt: discutir como resolver os problemas do mundo
items.section: C · Fixed expressions with set and put
items.example: We spent the evening putting the world to rights.
items.note: A common alternative to set the world to rights.

items.example: A careless visitor set fire to some dry grass.
items.note: Set fire to something means make it start burning.

items.example: The rescued birds were set free after recovering.
items.note: Set someone or something free means release them from captivity.

items.pt: pisar em; entrar em um lugar
items.example: She had never set foot in the laboratory before that day.
items.note: Often used in negative statements to emphasise never visiting a place.

items.example: The athlete set a new national record in the final.
items.note: Means establish a best officially recorded performance or result.

items.example: Managers should set a good example by following safety rules.
items.note: Means behave in a way that others can imitate positively.

items.example: The supervisor finally put her foot down about unsafe practices.
items.note: Means assert authority and refuse to permit something.

items.example: The deadline is putting pressure on the entire team.
items.note: Put pressure on someone means urge or force them to act, often insistently.

items.example: You can solve this problem if you really put your mind to it.
items.note: An idiom for directing serious mental effort towards a goal.

items.pt: ligar os pontos; chegar a uma conclusão óbvia
items.example: When the lights went out and the alarm sounded, we put two and two together.
items.note: Means infer what has happened from available clues.

items.example: The new policy aims to put an end to repeated delays.
items.note: Followed by a noun or -ing form; means stop something completely.

items.example: The organisers put a stop to the disruptive behaviour.
items.note: A close alternative to put an end to.

items.example: His dismissive tone really puts my back up.
items.note: An informal idiom meaning annoy someone, often by seeming disrespectful.

items.example: The supposedly spontaneous protest looked like a put-up job.
items.note: A noun meaning a deliberately arranged event intended to mislead people.

items.example: The unexpectedly high fee put me off joining the course.
items.note: Here, put off means discourage someone from doing something.

items.example: She put up her umbrella as soon as it began to rain.
items.note: Here, put up means raise or open an object such as an umbrella.

items.pt: vestir; colocar uma peça de roupa
items.example: He put on his jacket before leaving the office.
items.note: Put on clothes describes the action of getting dressed.

items.example: Each partner put in some money to launch the project.
items.note: Put money in a project means contribute or invest an amount.

items.example: She put in a lot of effort to improve her presentation.
items.note: Put in an effort means devote energy to an activity.

items.example: We set out at six to reach the station in time.
items.note: Set out can also mean begin a journey, like set off.

items.example: They put up a new picture in the meeting room.
items.note: Another common physical-object meaning of put up.

items.example: We put together a short summary from the interview notes.
items.note: An extended use of put together for combining information or materials.
